name: Navaneetheswarar Temple, Sikkal
deity: Shiva as Navaneetheswarar (Vennailingeswarar, the butter lingam), with the goddess Velnedungkanni
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung in the Tevaram; Singaravelan Murugan shrine within
summary: Sikkal, near Nagapattinam, honours Shiva as Navaneetheswarar — the lord of the butter lingam — a Paadal Petra Sthalam sung in the Tevaram, with the goddess Velnedungkanni. Within the same temple stands the famous shrine of Singaravelan, Murugan, where tradition holds that the goddess handed the lord his lance, the vel, before he set out to destroy the demon Surapadman. The twin presence of the butter-soft lingam and the warrior-god's vel gives Sikkal a devotion all its own.

sections.history: Sikkal is an old Shaiva temple near Nagapattinam, hymned in the seventh-century Tevaram and counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams of the southern Kaveri country. The stone temple carries Chola-period building with later additions. Over time the shrine of Murugan as Singaravelan grew to share the temple's fame equally with the Shiva sanctum, so that Sikkal is today a destination for devotees of both the lord of the butter lingam and the warrior-god of the vel.
sections.architecture: The complex follows the Dravidian plan, with the sanctum of Navaneetheswarar and the separate, celebrated shrine of Singaravelan Murugan within the same premises; the goddess Velnedungkanni has her own shrine. The lingam is revered as being soft as butter, giving the lord his name of Navaneetheswarar, the butter-lord. The Murugan shrine, with its bronze processional images, is the focus of the temple's most famous festival days.
sections.legends: The sthala-purana tells that the lingam here was fashioned from butter drawn from the milk of Kamadhenu by the sage Vasishta, so that the lord is the Navaneetheswarar, lord of butter. The temple's most celebrated tradition belongs to Murugan: it was here, the accounts say, that the goddess handed her son the vel, the divine lance, as he took up the command of the gods' army and set out to destroy the demon Surapadman, whom he vanquished at Tiruchendur the next day. The very name Sikkal is explained as 'the tangled place,' from obstacles overcome in the temple's making.
sections.festivals: The great festival of Sikkal is tied to Skanda Shashti in the Tamil month of Aippasi. On the day before Surasamharam, the image of Singaravelan receives the vel from the goddess — a moment awaited by vast crowds, when the bronze image is said to perspire with the intensity of the occasion. The Shaiva observances of Maha Shivaratri and Pradosham are also kept at the Navaneetheswarar sanctum.
sections.experience: Sikkal offers the pilgrim two devotions in one temple — the gentle grace of the butter lingam and the martial splendour of Singaravelan. On the vel-giving day the atmosphere is electric, the crowds immense; on ordinary days the temple is a calm place where the two currents of Shaiva worship, the contemplative and the heroic, meet.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Sikkal is about 7 km from Nagapattinam and near Tiruvarur; the nearest rail heads are Nagapattinam and Tiruvarur, with frequent buses and taxis to the temple.
